newsitem.title: USA: Marketers make up their Christmas lists.
newsitem.headline: Marketers make up their Christmas lists.

text.p: What do you want for Christmas? Madison Avenue marketers have a long list for you.
Here is what some of the leading marketers of consumer goods are doing in key product sectors to make your wish list look more like theirs:

LIQUOR: After stunning the American spirits industry and the public by ending its own 60-year old ban on electronic advertising, Joseph E. Seagram & Sons, the largest distiller, led others in dropping a voluntary industry code banning advertising on TV and radio.

But if television ads are creeping into the mix, print is still king. Seagram, the global marketer and distributor of Absolut vodka, will run ads in 150 magazines featuring a full-page board of 309 magnetic words in green that allow consumers to create their own messages on Absolut's artsy, collectible ads. Robert Bernstein, Absolut's senior marketing director says that based on early season distributor-to-retailer sales, "this should be a spectacular and typically late season."

ELECTRONICS - Sony Electronics, in Park Ridge, N.J., has let loose a number of new products for Christmas 1996 for its Walkman and other compact disc systems. But Sony is also making a big push for its new line of personal computers, its much-watched WebTV that allows simplified Internet access and a digital satellite system.

As its products become more sophisticated, Sony, with sales of $9 billion, is working harder to make its advertising more informational. It is using "advertorials" to explain its digital satellite systems to consumers in a group of consumer, trade and satellite publications, said Greg Gudorf, director of Sony's satellite TV sales. Sony has also launched its own credit card for those customers who buy at least $500 of Sony goods, and is also offering a free copy of the book, "What's On the Web."

COSMETICS - Lancome and Ralph Lauren fragrances, part of Cosmair Inc., New York, have boosted ad budgets and expect a solid payoff, says Jack Wiswall, senior vice president and general manager of Ralph Lauren Fragrances. "We're going much more American-festivity minded, meaning lifestyle and movie-style, in our presentation, graphics, counter displays, since we sense such a mood in the public."
Department stores, which are among Cosmair's biggest customers, have entered "a new, healthy environment and that means a healthy fragrance business this year," he said.
TOYS - With a beefed-up ad budget, new products and unusual samplings, the Hasbro Games Group, Pawtucket, R.I., expects to ring up a double-digit increase this Christmas season.

Bob Wann, Hasbro senior vice president, says that "Cybershot," an older kids' game, is one of Hasbro's major hopefuls this season even though it bears a relatively steep price-tag. It's a pin-ball, "extreme" hockey game played by two opponents.

"Kids like the extreme form of sports because it's exciting and competitive," Wann said. The game is being promoted in 250 roller rinks around the country where kids can play it and will be advertised primarily on television, as well as in specialised magazines.
Hasbro is also promoting its "Karate Fighters" game in a marketing tie-in with the World Wrestling Federation.

BOOKS - Random House, one of the American book industry's big publishers, has a trick up its sleeve -- or, rather, on the Internet. Images from the "Christmas Book," an illustrated volume that Random House hopes will become a holiday standard, have been put on its Website so surfers "can download them and make their own cards," said Deborah Aiges, vice president and creative director. Among the featured books will be a Picasso biography, flower photography by Robert Maplethorp and one on pickup trucks.

CLOTHES - After many months of unhappy business, the women's apparel business is starting to come alive with improved sales. It is counting on Christmas to sustain the uptrend, said Michael Dees, vice president of merchandising and design at Marisa Christina, Inc.

WATCHES - The Movado Group, based in Lyndhurst, N.J., has aggressively moved into the higher-ticket field by adding new features and more jewelry content. It is also pushing for the cyber addicts with its own Website.

"We are very encouraged by 1996 sales so far, which are up 14 percent for the first six months," said Movado Chairman Gerry Grinberg. "But we think it will be a very late shopping season. For watches, the Christmas week used to be a dead one years ago. Now, it's the year's biggest one."
